catalog_quote: [1991 p.51, sec. 2.1 Stress] Stress placement is very regular in Tomini-Tolitoli languages and thus empirically defines the domain of (word) phonology. It falls on the penultimate syllable of a (phonological) word and 'remains' penultimate when suffixes or clitics are added. Examples: 1a) bá'i 'head' b) ba'inye 'his/her head' Exceptions to this rule are very few in number and are dealt with in the following sections. [2001 p.73, sec. 3.4.8 Stress] Stress is usually not indicated, since it regularly falls on the penultimate syllable in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages. Only the exceptions to this rule are marked. Primary stress is marked by an acute accent <'>, secondary stress (i.e. lengthening of reduplicated syllables) by a grave accent. [2001 pp.91-92] The difference between suffixes and clitics/free forms is evident in stress assignment. Suffixed forms receive regular penultimate stress, i.e. the suffixes (all but one of which are monosyllables) cause the stress to move to the final syllable of the stem, while no such shift is triggered by clitics and free forms. [2001 p.92 fn.34] In Boano, a few words with possessive suffixes have been recorded in which stress clearly occurs on the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. báeku 'my house' (rather than baéku), báena 'his/her house', etc.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and non-contrastive: it falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word in Boano as in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages, and shifts rightward to stay penultimate when suffixes are added (clitics/free possessor forms do not trigger the shift per 2001 p.92).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 2001 p.73: 'secondary stress (i.e. lengthening of reduplicated syllables)' is marked with a grave accent in the word lists; no rhythmic secondary-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: General (group-wide): stress may move to the first member of a non-high+high vowel sequence (táipang ~ taípang, <10 of ~1200 items, 1991 sec. 2.5); shortened phonetically long vowels; Lauje paragogic /e/ and final-vowel drop yield surface antepenult/final stress. Boano-specific (2001 p.73): an overlong paragogic /e/ after word-final /y/ in about seven words does not shift stress (udoyE = údoye); (2001 p.92 fn.34): a few possessive-suffixed words recorded with antepenultimate stress (báeku 'my house', báena 'his/her house').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes (and, per 1991, clitics; 2001 p.92 distinguishes stress-shifting suffixes from non-shifting clitics/free forms). Data are elicited word-list/citation forms and paradigms from Himmelmann's 1988-93 fieldwork; the 1991 statement is a group-level generalisation over a sample that explicitly includes Boano, not a Boano-only description.
new_statements.identity_note: Himmelmann's 'Boano (Bolano)' is the Tomini-Tolitoli language spoken in the single village Bolano (Kec. Moutong, Tomini Bay coast), i.e. boan1243 / ISO bzl -- not Boano of Seram (boan1242), to which two items in Glottolog's boan1243 reference list (Collins 1982, Taber 1996) actually belong. The stress rule is stated for the Tomini-Tolitoli group as a whole (1991 sample explicitly lists Boano; 2001 says 'all Tomini-Tolitoli languages'), with Boano-specific remarks on exceptions (PL-511 p.73, p.92 fn.34).
